expert.item: Merge n intervals into the minimal disjoint set by sorting on start and extending or starting a new interval; the correctness invariant is that everything left of the cursor is already final.
The half-open overlap predicate s1 < e2 and s2 < e1, and the one tie rule it needs at a shared endpoint.

Inserting one interval into an already-merged, sorted list: find the first interval ending after the new one's start, absorb the run it overlaps, splice; O(n) by linear scan, O(log n + r) to find the place by binary search with the shifting still O(n).
Apache Flink's session windows as a real production instance of exactly this merge pass.
Maximum non-overlapping intervals: the earliest-finish-time greedy rule is optimal; earliest-start and shortest-first are not, and need running counter-examples.
The exchange argument that proves earliest-finish-time-first optimal (swap the optimal's first choice for the greedy one without losing size or creating overlap, then induct).
The fewest-conflicts-first rule also fails, on a separate, smaller counter-example than the one that beats earliest-start and shortest-first.
Unweighted maximum non-overlapping intervals is the unweighted case of maximum independent set in an interval graph.

Minimum number of rooms (interval partitioning) via a min-heap of end times: sort by start, reuse the earliest-ending room if it has already ended, else open a new one; the heap's final size is the answer.
Depth (the maximum overlap at any point) is a lower bound on rooms needed, and the heap algorithm always meets it, which is why it is optimal.
The same room count is produced by a simpler +1/-1 sweep over sorted endpoints with a running count; this is the bridge to the sweep line (topic 94).

Weighted interval scheduling: earliest-finish greedy fails once weights differ; the DP recurrence OPT(j) = max(OPT(j-1), w_j + OPT(p(j))) over intervals sorted by finish, with p(j) found by binary search, reconstructed by walking back; O(n log n) overall.
Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems (named with Chapter 22's vocabulary, declared here, not re-taught) and the exponential blow-up of the naive recursion against the memoised table.

Maximum-weight non-overlapping interval selection is polynomial, but the variant where each job offers several alternative time slots is NP-complete for three or more slots per job (claim to be confirmed against a primary source, not just Wikipedia, before it is stated on screen).

Interval trees answer a different, per-query question (which stored intervals overlap this query interval) than the batch questions this topic answers; named in post-notes, not built (Chapter 4, skipped).
Closed-interval conventions and other tie rules beyond the one this topic picks.
Interval joins in a database (IEJoin, sort-merge on two inequalities) and `de.point-in-time-as-of-joins` belong to Data Engineering.
